text: Lesson 17 set the rule that RPO determines minimum backup frequency. This lesson turns that number into an actual configured policy — Azure Backup policies, AWS Backup plans, retention, and the tiered retention pattern that keeps storage cost from growing forever.

An Azure Backup policy, attached to a Recovery Services vault, defines how often backups run and how long each one is kept. An AWS Backup plan does the same job across EBS volumes, RDS databases, and other resources from one place, instead of configuring snapshot schedules resource by resource. Both exist to turn a required frequency into something that runs on a schedule automatically.

Frequency and retention are two separate questions. Frequency is how often a backup is taken. Retention is how long a given backup sticks around before it's deleted. Keeping every backup forever sounds safe, but storage cost grows without bound, and most of those old recovery points are never actually restored from — the real skill is deciding how far back you genuinely need to recover.

The practical answer is tiered retention: dense backups for recent history, progressively sparser further back. A common pattern keeps daily backups for a week, weekly backups for a month, and monthly backups for a year. That gives fine-grained recovery points for the recent past, where you're most likely to need one, while older history stays recoverable at a coarser grain without paying to store 365 daily snapshots.

One policy doesn't fit every resource. A production database with a one-hour RPO needs a fundamentally different policy than a dev or test VM rebuilt from a template every sprint. Tagging resources and attaching different policies per tag is how real environments avoid over-backing-up low-value resources and under-backing-up the ones that actually matter. Next: testing a restore, because a backup that's never been test-restored might not actually work.
